posts.title: Fined for Going 8 mph
posts.topic: Walter Arnold, Jan 28 1896: 8 mph in a 2 mph zone, first speeding fine on record; limit raised to 14 mph later in 1896 (arrest/chase details left out on purpose)
slides: In 1896 a man drove his new motor car through a village at 8 mph. **The limit was 2.**
posts.caption:
He was fined, and it went down as the first speeding fine on record. Cars were so new the rules still treated them like steam engines. By the end of that same year the limit jumped to 14 mph. Could you stand a week at 2?

#JuryJuice #SpeedingTicket #ClassicCars

posts.title: Fined $500 for Doing the Math
posts.topic: Järlström v. Aldridge: after wife's red-light camera ticket (2013) he studied yellow-light timing; state engineering board fined him $500 for calling himself an engineer; state admitted First Amendment violation and offered refund (2017); judge ruled board's rules overbroad (Dec 28 2018)
slides: He did the math on his wife's red-light camera ticket. Then the state fined him $500 **for calling himself an engineer.**
posts.caption:
So he sued the board in federal court. The state admitted it had violated his free-speech rights and offered his $500 back. In 2018 a judge went further and said the rules on who gets to use the word engineer reached way too far. It all began with a tenth of a second at a yellow light. Ever timed one yourself?

posts.title: $18,000 Hidden in a Plane Wing
posts.topic: Benjamin v. Lindner Aviation (Iowa 1995): mechanic found ~$18,000 (mostly 1950s bills) behind a wing panel during a 1992 inspection; money turned over to police; no owner claimed it in 12 months; mechanic, repair shop and bank (plane's owner) all claimed; mislaid property, all to the bank; trial court's 10% finder's fee reversed. Mechanic's first attempt to split the cash left out on purpose.
slides: A mechanic opened up a plane's wing and found **$18,000 in old cash**.
The bills were decades old, tucked behind a panel held on by **rusty screws**.
The cash was turned over to the police. A year later, **nobody had claimed it**.
Now the mechanic, the repair shop and the bank that owned the plane all wanted it.
The highest court in the state gave every dollar to the plane's owner. **The mechanic got nothing.**
Follow for more
posts.caption:
Finders keepers lost this one. If you found cash inside something you were fixing, whose money would it be?

#JuryJuice #LostAndFound #FoundMoney

posts.title: Radar Clocked the Trees at 86 mph
posts.topic: 1979 Dade County radar hearings: WTVJ series showed radar clocking a stand of trees at 86 mph and a house at 28 mph (UPI); ~4,000 radar speeding cases postponed; Judge Alfred Nesbitt (not named) ruled radar alone too unreliable to convict; 80 radar cases dismissed
slides: A TV crew aimed a police radar gun at a row of trees. It read **86 mph**. Drivers fighting speeding tickets took that to a judge.
posts.caption:
He agreed with them. In 1979 he decided a radar reading alone wasn't reliable enough to prove anyone was speeding, and 80 radar cases were dismissed. About 4,000 more had been put on hold waiting for his answer. Do you trust the number on those roadside speed signs?

#JuryJuice #SpeedingTicket #RadarGun

Sources: UPI (1979); University Daily Kansan

posts.title: A Physics Paper vs. a Stop-Sign Ticket
posts.topic: 2012: physicist Dmitri Krioukov (not named) got a $400 ticket for not stopping at a stop sign; wrote 4-page paper 'The Proof of Innocence'; ticket dismissed; commissioner Karen Riley said decision was not based on physics but on the officer's view (too far from intersection)
slides: An officer said a physicist never fully stopped at the stop sign. He fought the **$400 ticket** in court with a four-page physics paper.
posts.caption:
He won, though the court commissioner said later that most of the physics went over her head. She dropped the ticket because the officer had been too far from the corner to see it clearly. Would a paper like that have convinced you?

posts.title: The NULL License Plate
posts.topic: Joseph Tartaro (not named), security researcher, vanity plate NULL; ticket processing system matched tickets with missing plate data to his plate; over $12,000 in other people's citations; processing center canceled the $12,000, ~$6,000 more still showed later; DMV and LAPD told him to change the plate (DEF CON 2019). Framed as a programmer's joke, not as a way to dodge tickets.
slides: His license plate said NULL, a programmer's joke. Computers mailed him **$12,000 in strangers' tickets** before that bill got canceled.
posts.caption:
The fix both the DMV and police offered was simple: change the plate. Could you give up a plate like that?

posts.title: 3 Times the Defendant Was an Object
posts.topic: In rem cases: US v. One Solid Gold Object in Form of a Rooster (D. Nev. 1962, 206.3 troy oz restaurant statue, Gold Reserve Act 50 oz limit, jury for owner, returned); US v. 95 Barrels Alleged Apple Cider Vinegar (1924, unanimous, dried-apple vinegar misbranded); US v. Approximately 64,695 Pounds of Shark Fins (9th Cir. 2008, KD II not a fishing vessel, fins returned). Casino and nationalities left out on purpose.
slides: 3 real court cases where **the defendant was an object**
In 1962, **a solid gold rooster** was the defendant. A jury ruled for it, and it went back to its restaurant.
**95 barrels of vinegar** reached the nation's top court in 1924. Not one justice sided with the seller.
Officials took **32 tons of shark fins** off one ship. In 2008, an appeals court gave them back.
Follow for more
posts.caption:
A rooster, some vinegar and 32 tons of fins each got their day in court. Which case surprised you most?
